subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which type of wave is most associated with deposition and the building up of a beach?
questions.explain: Constructive waves have a strong swash and weak backwash, so they deposit material and build up the beach.

questions.q: What is the name of the erosion process in which the sheer force of moving water compresses air in cracks and breaks off rock?
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is the force of waves compressing air in cracks, weakening and breaking the rock apart.

questions.q: During attrition, what happens to the rock fragments carried by the sea?
options: They become smaller and rounder as they collide
They dissolve into the sea water
They are hurled against the cliff face
They are lifted and carried in suspension
questions.explain: In attrition, rock fragments knock against each other and gradually become smaller and more rounded.

questions.q: Why does longshore drift move material along a beach in a zig-zag pattern?
options: Swash carries material up the beach at an angle, while backwash pulls it straight back down
Waves approach the shore at right angles at all times
The tide carries material out to sea and back again
Wind blows the material directly along the shoreline
questions.explain: The swash follows the angle of the prevailing wind while the backwash returns at right angles under gravity, creating a zig-zag movement.

questions.q: Which combination best describes a destructive wave?
options: High energy, weak swash and strong backwash
Low energy, strong swash and weak backwash
High energy, strong swash and weak backwash
Low energy, weak swash and strong backwash
questions.explain: Destructive waves are high-energy with a weak swash and strong backwash, so they remove material and erode the coast.

questions.q: Solution (corrosion) as a coastal erosion process most affects which type of rock?
questions.explain: Solution occurs when slightly acidic sea water dissolves soluble rocks such as limestone and chalk.

questions.q: Sand grains bouncing along the sea bed are being transported by which process?
questions.explain: Saltation is the bouncing or hopping movement of small particles along the sea bed.

questions.q: Why do headlands and bays form along a coastline of alternating hard and soft rock?
options: Softer rock is eroded faster to form bays, leaving harder rock as headlands
Harder rock is eroded faster to form bays, leaving softer rock as headlands
Deposition builds up headlands while erosion creates bays
Both rock types erode at the same rate but wind shapes the coast
questions.explain: Less resistant rock erodes quickly to form bays, while the more resistant rock is left protruding as headlands.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence in the formation of a stack from a headland?
questions.explain: Erosion enlarges a crack into a cave, then an arch, which collapses to leave a stack that eventually erodes to a stump.

questions.q: How is a wave-cut platform formed?
options: Waves erode a notch at the cliff base, the cliff collapses and retreats, leaving a rocky platform
Deposited sediment builds up a flat rocky surface at low tide
A stack collapses and spreads out to form a flat rock surface
Longshore drift deposits material to create a level shelf
questions.explain: Erosion forms a wave-cut notch; as the cliff retreats, the gently sloping wave-cut platform is left behind.

questions.q: Which coastal landform is a ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end with a recurved (hooked) end?
questions.explain: A spit is a depositional feature extending from the coast, often with a recurved end shaped by changing wind direction.

questions.q: A ridge of shingle has grown across the mouth of a bay, trapping fresh water behind it to form a lagoon. What landform is this?
questions.explain: When a spit grows completely across a bay it forms a bar, enclosing a lagoon behind it.

questions.q: Loose material builds up where a river or coastline suddenly changes direction, and longshore drift continues to deposit sediment out into open water. Which feature is most likely to develop?
questions.explain: Where the coastline changes direction, longshore drift deposits material into the open water, building a spit.

questions.q: Which of the following is a depositional landform rather than an erosional one?
questions.explain: A beach is formed by the deposition of sand and shingle, whereas arches, stacks and wave-cut platforms result from erosion.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of hard engineering coastal management?
questions.explain: A sea wall is a hard-engineering structure built to reflect wave energy and protect the coast.

questions.q: How do groynes help to protect a beach?
options: They trap sediment moved by longshore drift, building up the beach
They reflect wave energy back out to sea
They dissolve wave energy by absorbing it into wire cages
They add new sand to replace eroded material
questions.explain: Groynes are barriers that interrupt longshore drift, trapping sediment and widening the beach so it absorbs wave energy.

questions.q: What does the soft-engineering technique of beach nourishment involve?
options: Adding sand or shingle to a beach to replace eroded material
Building a concrete barrier along the shoreline
Placing large boulders at the base of a cliff
Allowing low-lying land to be flooded by the sea
questions.explain: Beach nourishment replaces lost sediment, creating a wider beach that absorbs wave energy naturally.

questions.q: Rock armour (rip rap) reduces erosion by which method?
options: Absorbing and dissipating wave energy at the cliff base
Trapping sediment carried by longshore drift
Reflecting all wave energy straight back out to sea
Draining water away from behind the cliff
questions.explain: Rock armour consists of large boulders that break up and absorb wave energy before it reaches the cliff.

questions.q: A council wants a low-cost, natural-looking method that works with the environment to protect a stretch of dune coastline. Which option best fits?
questions.explain: Dune regeneration is a soft-engineering approach that restores natural dunes to absorb wave energy at low cost.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Geography (2017) specification; Coastal Environments
